paras: The Radford Fair Grounds lynching threat was an episode on July 4, 1903, at the races in Radford, Virginia, in which a crowd cried for the lynching of an unnamed Black man accused of striking a white man with a whip. A former United States marshal quieted the crowd and a sergeant took the man to jail, and no injury to him was reported. Richmond and Washington papers reported it as violence narrowly averted.
According to a special dispatch to the Richmond Times-Dispatch, Radford was crowded on the Fourth of July, and order held at the well-attended Fair Grounds races until late evening.

At the end of the second heat of the last race, the Black man was said to have struck a white man, Joskey Brown, "over the head and face with a whip." Because Brown was small, the correspondent wrote, the crowd pressed in, and "some thoughtless persons cried lynch him." Joseph R. Jordan, an ex-United States marshal, quelled the crowd for the moment, and when Sergeant McNeal arrived the man was "hustled off to the jail" in the sergeant's buggy.
No report of a charge, hearing or outcome for the jailed man appears in the coverage, and his name was not given.

The Times-Dispatch ran the special under the headline "EXCITEMENT IN RADFORD," with the deck "Angry and Excited Crowd Came Near Doing Violence to a Negro." Its Virginia news summary in the same issue described "a row between a negro and a white jocky" that came near ending in violence to the Black man. It called those who cried for lynching "thoughtless."

On July 6 the Washington Times reduced the story to two sentences, saying the man "started a small riot" and officers frustrated a threatened lynching. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The white man appears as "Joskey Brown" in the Times-Dispatch and "Jockey Brown" in the Washington Times; the Times-Dispatch summary calls him a white jockey. The Washington Times called the disorder "a small riot," while the fuller Virginia dispatch describes only an angry crowd pressing in.

reader.title: Radford Fair Grounds lynching threat
bases: A crowd cried 'lynch him' and pressed in on a Black man accused of whipping a white man, and was held back by an ex-marshal and officers; no one was harmed (A2, A3).
A crowd threatened to lynch the man over his alleged attack on a white man, but he was taken to jail and no one was killed (A2, A3); this was a threatened lynching, not a completed one.

The Times-Dispatch special (A2, with its digest line A1) and the Washington Times brief (A3) agree on the whip-strike at the Radford races, the lynching threat and its prevention, though A3 is short and may derive from a Virginia report.

accounts.label: Times-Dispatch special correspondent
accounts.gist: A Black man whipped the small white man Brown after a heat; the crowd pressed in and some cried 'lynch him' until Jordan quieted them and McNeal took the man to jail.

accounts.label: Washington Times brief
accounts.gist: The whip-strike on 'Jockey Brown' started 'a small riot', and the officers frustrated a threatened lynching.

framing.detail: Headlined 'EXCITEMENT IN RADFORD / Angry and Excited Crowd Came Near Doing Violence to a Negro', it called those crying lynch 'thoughtless persons' while presenting the whip-strike as fact.
The state news digest summarized it as a row between a Black man and a white jockey that came near ending in violence to the Black man.
A two-sentence item stating the Black man 'started a small riot' and that officers frustrated a threatened lynching.

conflicts.note: Likely the same man; 'Jockey' may be his occupation or a misreading, since the digest calls him a white jockey.
